extracted.intended_audience: serious readers, literary critics, and novelists (students of fiction)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the craft and criticism of the modern novel: how to read 'aright', how novels are made (selection, arrangement, point of view, scene vs picture, etc.), and how to judge their form and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: A book has a form (shape/design)
rubrics_metrics.description: A book has a certain form, a shape ascribable to it; its form may be 'good' or 'bad' and is the material object one should attempt to perceive and judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek the novel’s overall shape by reconstructing it as a single, welded mass rather than only as a succession of scenes; ask whether the form expresses the subject and whether defects of form indicate defects in treatment or subject. Recognize that memory and reading habits make this difficult, so deliberate reconstruction is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read aright / creative reading
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning of criticism is to read aright: the reader must actively recreate the book in his mind rather than passively consume its life-like effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice 'creative reading' (Emerson’s phrase): hold the novel at a distance, collect impressions deliberately, and construct a coherent image of the book page by page so that its form and design become visible for critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and arrangement by novelist
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist’s craft consists largely in selection and arrangement—choosing, disengaging, and completing fragments of life and disposing them in a single embracing design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the author’s choices (what is included, emphasized, omitted) serve the subject; evaluate how selections are arranged to produce unity or to diffuse the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character and imaginative gift (truth to life)
rubrics_metrics.description: A central evaluative criterion is the novelist’s command of life: the power to render convincing, vivid, and true characters and human situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the author’s grasp of character, range, depth, and how the imaginative gifts sustain the life-like effects that form the core of a novel’s value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form vs life (balance of design and life-like energy)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is tension between formal design and the novel’s life-like immediacy; a novel may be badly constructed yet full of life, and the importance of form varies in fiction compared with other arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging, weigh both design and vitality: ask whether defects of form truly impair the work’s effect or whether the life in the book compensates. But do not dismiss form; examine where it matters for expressing the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: The dramatic scene (dramatic incident) as primary instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic scene is a chief instrument of the novelist—'the scene, properly so called—this comes first in importance.' It delivers the final, decisive stroke in a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scenes sparingly and strategically: place fully wrought scenes where they clinch matters already pending; avoid wasting scenes on tasks they cannot economically accomplish. Evaluate placement and preparation of scenes for maximum effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture/panoramic/general survey (pictorial mode)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictorial or panoramic methods give breadth over time and space and accumulate impression; they are preliminary and preparatory relative to dramatic scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the novelist’s use of pictorial narration for broad reaches and accumulated impression; determine whether picture and panorama complement or diffuse the dramatic structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of time and space (scenic cost)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene cannot compress more time or space than it represents; it is 'expensive' in time and space compared with summary or narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the author uses dramatic presentation where it is justified; consider whether oblique narrative or summary could achieve the same effect more economically and whether the scene is adequately prepared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and placement of scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene must be prepared in advance to avoid wasting its strength; scenes should gather and crown effects made by other means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether scenes are set up by prior narrative or pictorial work so that they act swiftly and sharply; look for scenes that integrate multiple issues and advance the story without forced effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative uses of narrative modes (technical awareness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative employs several modes—dramatic, pictorial, scenic, generalized, panoramic—each with different properties and appropriate uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which modes are being used and whether they are the appropriate instruments for the stage of the story; be attentive to how modes combine and to the novelist’s working theory of their relative values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of time and space
rubrics_metrics.description: Different methods of narration handle time and space differently (scenes show entire time and space; narrative or summary can cover long spans economically).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how the author compresses or expands time, whether transitions are managed smoothly, and whether the technique chosen serves the subject’s demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view / presence between author and reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Point of view (the position through which the story is presented) is crucial: whether the author speaks directly, or interposes a consciousness or narrator affects strength and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the appropriateness and consistency of the chosen point of view; note advantages of centering a story in a fashioned mind (consciousness) and dangers of arbitrary or inconsistent shifts. Consider the effects of omniscience vs limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of consciousness / dramatized mind
rubrics_metrics.description: A story filtered through somebody’s consciousness—'the story that is centred in somebody’s consciousness'—can convert pictorial weakness into dramatic strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for how effectively the novelist constructs and sustains a constituted mind as a theatrical or dramatized presence; judge whether this enhances vividness and unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and coherence (welded mass)
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful novel should leave, in the reader’s mind, a single, coherent, appraisable book rather than a mere procession of disconnected scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recreate the book’s overall design after reading; test whether chapters fit into an ordered whole and whether the subject is consistently and compactly expressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment must fit the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of treatment must arise from the subject: the right mode and development depend on what the subject requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the author started from the heart of the subject and has followed its natural development; when treatment diverges, identify whether the fault lies in theory, method, or in a poor/unfruitful subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of incidents for clarity of drama
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist selects figures and incidents for the clarity with which they embody the drama or subject (e.g., selecting figures to represent generational drama).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the appropriateness of chosen incidents and characters as embodiments of the book’s central thought or theme; consider whether selection clarifies or dilutes the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial freedom vs disciplined method ('minstrel’s licence' critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author may take a free, minstrel-like licence of voice and digression, but the critic warns that 'the easiest way is no way'—discipline and method generally produce more of the story’s potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh authorial digressions and liberties: where license enhances the book’s character it may be appropriate; but check whether laxity curtails the fullest expression of the subject and whether a more disciplined method would have made more of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid shyness in analysis of novels
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics often shy away from dissecting novels because they are 'pieces of life,' but a novel should be treated as a piece of art and examined technically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be deterred by the illusion of life; analyze technical aspects—form, modes, selection, handling of scenes—without romantic scruple to see how the book is made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert method's disabilities into strengths (mirror/mind metaphor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Admit a method’s inherent weaknesses (e.g., pictorial thinness) and use them deliberately—for example, by dramatizing the mind that mirrors events to create a distinct effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify apparent limitations of a technique and ask whether the author has exploited them creatively (e.g., turning pictorial report into compelling presentation by making the narrator’s mind itself visible and dramatic).

rubrics_metrics.name: The critic as co-creator/novelist (reader responsibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: The critical reader is also a maker of the book in his mind and must take responsibility to construct the form the author intended or made possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be an active participant: collect, shape, and test the impressions; recreate the book with deliberation so that critical judgments about form and method are grounded in a reconstructed whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical vocabulary and acuity (need for precise terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical vocabulary for types of narrative (dramatic, pictorial, scenic, generalized, panoramic) is underdeveloped and criticism suffers; technical awareness is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and use precise critical terms; when classifying mode or effect, define what is meant (e.g., 'dramatic narrative' vs 'pictorial narrative') and apply consistently in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene’s limitations: cannot shorten time/cover expansive matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene shows the whole of the time and space it occupies; it cannot imply more than it renders, unlike summary which can suggest long periods economically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve fully dramatized scenes for moments that demand vivid, immediate rendering and rely on narrative summary where breadth and economy are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of judging treatment in detail (workmanlike handling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond recognizing forms and modes, the critic must inspect the novelist’s detailed workmanship—how he handles transitions, preparations, and the specific uses of narrative devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine precisely how effects are achieved: distribution of emphasis, texture of scenes, rhythm of narration, and how parts cohere technically to the whole.
